# Postgres-backed claims: queues, atomic staging, verifier checks

The bundled postgres claim producer turns a database into a claim substrate. It
hands each claimant a distinct row from a queue, stages a batch and swaps it in
whole, checks a staged batch before letting it land, and declares error classes
a template can subscribe to.

## Two producers over one database

One producer is configured for synchronous writes with a pick policy;
the other for staged-async writes with its verifier executor enabled.

`cp-queue.yml`:

```yaml
connection: "postgres://store:store@substrate-pg:5432/storedb?sslmode=disable"
write_semantics: sync
host: 0.0.0.0
grpc_port: 9101
http_port: 9111
sweep_interval_seconds: 30
pick_policies:
  "@queue":
    items_table: work_items
    on_commit: pop
    on_give_up: recycle
    visibility_timeout_seconds: 300
```

`cp-staged.yml`:

```yaml
connection: "postgres://store:store@substrate-pg:5432/storedb?sslmode=disable"
write_semantics: staged_async
host: 0.0.0.0
grpc_port: 9101
http_port: 9111
sweep_interval_seconds: 30
enable_executor: true
```

The deployment names both, and names the staged producer's executor endpoint as
an executor of its own:

```yaml
claim_producers:
  "queue-store":
    endpoint: "grpc://cp-queue:9101"
    write_semantics_allowed: ["sync"]
  "staged-store":
    endpoint: "grpc://cp-staged:9101"
    write_semantics_allowed: ["staged_async"]

executors:
  "pg-verifier":
    transport: grpc
    endpoint: "grpc://cp-staged:9101"
```

The items table the pick policy reads:

```sql
CREATE TABLE work_items (
  item_id     TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  payload     JSONB NOT NULL,
  state       TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'available',
  claim_token TEXT,
  claimed_at  TIMESTAMPTZ,
  enqueued_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
  priority    INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  sequence    BIGSERIAL
);

INSERT INTO work_items (item_id, payload, priority) VALUES
  ('job-alpha', '{"topic":"alpha"}', 10),
  ('job-beta',  '{"topic":"beta"}',  5);
```

## Each claimant gets a different row

```yaml
name: pg-queue-pick
version: v1
nodes:
  - type: worker
    executor: http-node
    claim_producers:
      - name: queue-store
        selector: "@queue"
        intent: rw
        alias: item
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable": {action: give_up}
      "pg/claim_unavailable": {action: give_up}
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:     {type: string, default: "http://sqlwriter:19489/rec/worker"}
          method:  {type: string, default: POST}
          item_id: {type: string, source: "{{claim.item.address}}"}
          topic:   {type: string, source: "{{claim.item.payload.topic}}"}
```

Create two instances of this template. The first claimant receives `job-alpha`
and the second `job-beta`, each with its own row's payload substituted into its
dispatch. Both claim handles record realized write semantics `sync`.

Two workers pulling from one queue do not collide on the same item, and the
operator declares that behaviour as producer configuration rather than building
it into the template.

## A drained queue fires a class you can subscribe to

Add a node that subscribes to the producer's class namespace:

```yaml
  - type: watcher
    executor: http-node
    subscribes:
      - node: worker
        type: terminal/error/pg/*
        force_upstream_refresh: false
```

A third claim against the drained policy settles the claiming node on
`terminal/error/pg/claim_unavailable`, and the watcher runs on that signal.

The producer advertises exactly three error classes — claim-unavailable,
swap-failed, and not-atomically-replaceable. Read them off
`GET /v1/observability/claim-producers/{name}`.

A canonical schema carrying an external dependent settles its claiming node on
the not-atomically-replaceable class, and the schema and its dependent are left
untouched: the refusal is a refusal, not a partial change.

## A batch becomes visible whole, or not at all

```yaml
name: pg-staged-pass
version: v1
nodes:
  - type: stager
    executor: http-node
    claim_producers:
      - name: staged-store
        selector: analytics_production
        intent: rw
        alias: staged
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable": {action: give_up}
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:    {type: string, default: "http://sqlwriter:19489/stage"}
          method: {type: string, default: POST}
          staging_schema: {type: string, source: "{{claim.staged.address}}"}
          rows:   {type: integer, default: 10}

  - type: verifier
    executor: pg-verifier
    holds:
      staged: {from: stager}
    subscribes:
      - node: stager
        type: terminal/success
        force_upstream_refresh: false
    error_types:
      "pg/verifier_check_failed/row_count_ratio": {action: give_up}
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          schema: {type: string, source: "{{claim.staged.address}}"}
          table:  {type: string, default: items}
          checks:
            type: array
            default:
              - kind: row_count_ratio
                config: {baseline: 10, low: 0.9, high: 1.1}

  - type: watcher
    executor: http-node
    subscribes:
      - node: verifier
        type: terminal/error/pg/*
        force_upstream_refresh: false
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:    {type: string, default: "http://sqlwriter:19489/rec/watcher"}
          method: {type: string, default: POST}
```

The claim on the canonical schema `analytics_production` resolves to a staging
address distinct from it — a `rimsky_stg_…` schema — and the claim handle
records `staged_async` rather than quietly downgrading to `sync`. The advertised
behaviour is the realized one.

The stager writes ten rows into the staging schema. After commit, the canonical
schema holds those ten rows in place of the single row it started with, and the
staging schema no longer exists: the commit swapped the content in rather than
copying it row by row. A reader of the canonical schema sees the old batch or
the new one, never a half-written mixture.

## A staged batch is checked before it lands

The `verifier` node above co-holds the staged claim and runs a
`row_count_ratio` check over the staged content against a baseline of ten. For
the ten-row batch it passes.

Run the same shape where the stager writes only two rows. The checking node
settles on the producer's per-check class,
`terminal/error/pg/verifier_check_failed/row_count_ratio`, and the watcher
subscribing to `terminal/error/pg/*` runs on that signal. The check is both a
gate on the batch and an event a template can react to.

The per-check class is subscribable but is not among the three classes the
producer advertises, so an operator enumerating the advertised classes will not
find it there.
